articles.title: 'You can almost see the panic in Trump's eyes' in his latest scramble: MS NOW host
articles.description: Donald Trump appears to be wearing down due to daily trips to campaign in states where Republican lawmakers normally would be gliding to victory in the upcoming midterm election. That is according to MS NOW host Stephanie Ruhle who suggested on Friday morning that the president looks desperate to forestall what is expected to be a Republican Party "bloodbath" in eleven days. “We are just 11 days away from the midterms, Ruhle reminded her audience before adding, “As we come on the air today, I want to zoom in on the Republican anxiety over some of these red state Senate races. You can almost see the panic in Donald Trump's eyes when you look at his upcoming travel schedule.” She noted, “Donald Trump tonight heads to Florida, a state he won by 13 points in 2024. Monday, he's headed to Mississippi, where he won by 22 points. And Tuesday he's headed back to Texas, where, of course, he won by 13 points. And on Wednesday he's headed to Ohio, which he won by 11 points.” “Of course, the most shocking part of that travel itinerary has got to be Mississippi, where Democrats are spending more than $1 million for a late ad boost,” she continued before adding, “The state has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since Ronald Reagan was president.”

articles.title: This red state race could spell big trouble for MAGA's post-Trump future: column
articles.description: An instantly infamous Republican attack ad in Ohio may be exposing deep fault lines over what comes after Donald Trump, according to an analysis. In a new column, New York Times columnist Michelle Goldberg wrote that Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP nominee for Ohio governor, released “what may be the most disgusting ad in American political history.” In doing so, Goldberg argued, he opened “a kind of proxy debate on the right about whether a post-Trump conservatism should try to reclaim some base-line morality or continue along its current smashmouth course.” The ad features the elderly mother of Democratic nominee Amy Acton calling her daughter a liar. Acton was 12 when her stepfather was indicted on charges of raping her. He fled before trial, and her mother stood by him, lost custody of her children and has not seen Acton since 1978. The spot first circulated online without attribution, but as outrage mounted, Ramaswamy’s campaign admitted it was behind the ad, then, “in Trumpian style, doubled down,” vowing to spend millions to air it. “By tacitly siding with a man indicted on charges of child rape," Goldberg wrote, "Ramaswamy has shown us all who he is." Some of the sharpest criticism has come from the right. National Review, which published its “Against Trump” issue in 2016 before becoming one of the president’s “apologists and bootlickers,” Goldberg wrote, has now run several columns lambasting Ramaswamy. Conservative commentator Erick Erickson, who endorsed Trump in 2019 despite misgivings, lamented, “We keep being told we must surrender our decency to win and then we lament how indecent the country is becoming," but Goldberg jabbed that he wrote this “as if he had not been one of the ones counseling such surrender.” Trump and Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, rallied behind the ad. Vance praised Ramaswamy’s “audacity” and scoffed at Republicans “whining” about it. Trump wrote that he wished “the mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse.” “Both men seem to understand that Republicans who criticize Ramaswamy are also implicitly criticizing them,” Goldberg wrote. That’s especially true for Vance, Ramaswamy’s friend from Yale Law School, who shares his venture capital and tech-right résumé. Goldberg branded both men “charmless, awkwardly imitating the president’s cruel provocations without his dark charisma or comic timing.” With Trump so unpopular that Republicans risk losing Texas and Kansas, and “the whole gaudy edifice of MAGA” crumbling, the stakes go well beyond Ohio. “If Ramaswamy loses a state as red as Ohio despite Trump’s imprimatur, Vance might start to look like a bad bet in 2028,” Goldberg warned.

articles.title: Giorgia Meloni is Italy’s great political survivor. Could one man be about to bring her down? | Riccardo Alcaro
articles.description: With elections looming in 2027, Roberto Vannacci’s new far-right movement could fatally outflank the prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s government became the longest serving in Italy’s republican history last month. This unusual political longevity, a moderate foreign policy, a certain personal charisma and even a recent spat with Donald Trump have combined to sharpen Meloni’s profile as the go-to leader on the European right. Meloni’s personal approval rating – at about 41% – is one of the highest among west European leaders. Her far-right Brothers of Italy party has retained most of its support – a striking feat in our anti-incumbent era and by Italian standards, an achievement.
